paper_title: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Chunk-Interleaved Full-Duplex Speech Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Chunk-interleaved full-duplex speech language models listen and speak in fixed time chunks, and each chunk must be processed before the next one arrives. Their workload is asymmetric across chunks: listen chunks leave compute idle while awaiting audio, and speak and tool-call chunks require serial generation, which delays responses and tool calls. Using the idle compute for the next chunk requires decoding it before its audio arrives, under an assumed input. Taking silence as the assumed input and comparing the output with the output under real audio on four models, we observe two properties. First, the next audio chunk does not change the output in 95.3% of chunks. Second, 88% of changes begin at the first output token. Building on these properties, we propose Speculative Listening, a training-free, lossless framework for input-time self-speculative decoding. During idle time, the model drafts the next chunk under silence and, for changes at the first token, a second branch from the runner-up first token. It keeps all drafts in a cross-chunk hypothesis pool and verifies them when the audio arrives. On our eight-task benchmark TickTock-Bench, Speculative Listening speeds up speak chunks by 2.6-2.8x and tool-call chunks by up to 23.4x. On average, it reduces the decoding delay before a response starts by 73%, to 74-241 ms, close to the 200 ms gap between human turns, and the maximum lag behind real time by 94.4%.

On our eight-task benchmark TickTockBench, Speculative Listening speeds up speak chunks by 2.62.8 and tool-call chunks by up to 23.4. On average, it reduces the decoding delay before response starts by 73%, to 74241 ms, close to the 200 ms gap between human turns, and the maximum lag behind real time by 94.4%. 1. Introduction Full-duplex speech language models listen and speak at the same time (Defossez et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2026; Think1The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, China 2Amphion Technology Co., Ltd. Correspondence to: Yutong Bian <yutongbian02@gmail.com>, Zhizheng Wu <wuzhizheng@cuhk.edu.cn>. Preprint. November 6, 2026. Figure 1. Decoding in chunk-interleaved full-duplex speech language model. (a) Autoregressive decoding leaves compute idle while it waits for audio, and long output then misses the chunk deadline. (b) Speculative Listening drafts the next chunk under silence during the idle window and verifies the whole draft in one forward pass when the audio arrives. ing Machines Lab, 2026). widely adopted design is the chunk-interleaved architecture (Zhang et al., 2024b; Cui et al., 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026; Orantqing et al., 2026; Ant Group, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), which divides streaming conversation into fixed time chunks (Figure 1). In each chunk, the model processes the newly arrived audio and decodes its output, which may keep listening, speak, or call tool (Orantqing et al., 2026; Ant Group, 2026). The audio of the next chunk arrives in real time, and the chunk duration acts as hard deadline (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026): chunk that takes longer to decode delays the following chunks, and the conversation lags behind real time. The model then processes the users speech late, and its responses become stale in the ongoing interaction. Profiling four chunk-interleaved models chunk by chunk (Figure 3a), we find their workload asymmetric across chunks. Listen chunks only process the newly arrived audio and leave compute idle for 7089% of the chunk duration while awaiting the next audio chunk (Figure 1a). We call this unused time the idle window. Speak and tool-call chunks require serial generation, and its length grows with the output: long output, such as tool call, takes tens of serial forward passes (Figure 4a), each bound by the memory bandwidth of loading model weights and the KV cache (Shazeer, 2019). Tool-call chunks miss the deadline, and model with written channel decoded alongside speech (Zhang et al., 2026) misses it on 95% of speak chunks. Decoding also delays Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models the start of each response: under AR, it adds 4171089 ms on average. Human speakers respond about 200 ms after the other speaker ends (Levinson & Torreira, 2015). Prior work addresses neighbouring parts of this problem. Lossless speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) accelerates serial generation with draft models (Li et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024) or context lookup (Saxena, 2023; Luo et al., 2025) once the input is available. Recent speech systems compute during listening windows by training the model to emit reasoning tokens (Wu et al., 2026) or by pre-generating candidate responses in turn-based cascaded pipelines (Li & Grover, 2025). In end-to-end chunkinterleaved models, the idle window has not yet been used to decode the output of the next chunk. Using the idle window requires decoding chunk before its audio arrives, that is, under an assumed input. We take silence as the simplest assumption, which we call the silence hypothesis, and at every chunk across four models decode the output twice: once with the real audio and once with the audio replaced by silence (Section 3.2). Comparing the two outputs, we observe two properties (Figure 3b,c): 1. The next audio chunk usually does not change the output. The output under silence matches the real-audio output token for token in 95.3% of chunks pooled over the four models. 2. When the output changes, it diverges at the first token. Pooled over the four models, 88% of divergences occur at the first output token, where most of the models decide to stay silent or start responding. Building on these properties, we propose Speculative Listening, training-free and lossless framework for input-time self-speculative decoding (Figure 1b and Figure 2). During the idle window, the target model drafts the upcoming chunk under the silence hypothesis and keeps the drafts of all earlier chunks in cross-chunk hypothesis pool (Fu et al., 2024). second draft branch, started from the runner-up first token, covers divergences at the first token. When the real audio arrives, one forward pass processes it and verifies the whole draft. If the output departs from the draft, later forward passes continue from matching draft in the pool, such as the runner-up branch. Post-audio computation then grows only with changed tokens (Section 3.3). We also introduce TickTock-Bench, Spec-Benchinspired (Xia et al., 2024) unified benchmark and replay harness for full-duplex decoding under chunk deadlines. It covers eight reasoning, conversation, and agentic tasks (Section 4). Experiments on four models show that Speculative Listening speeds up speak chunks by 2.62.8 on average and tool-call chunks by up to 23.4 (Figure 6b), reduces the maximum lag behind real time by 94.4% on average  (Table 3)  , and shortens the decoding delay before response starts by 73% on average, to 74241 ms (Section 5.4). Our contributions are three-fold: We identify two properties of chunk outputs in chunkinterleaved full-duplex models: the next audio chunk usually does not change the output, and changes concentrate at the first output token. We propose Speculative Listening, training-free and lossless decoding framework whose post-audio computation grows only with changed tokens, and which stays faster than autoregressive decoding under stochastic sampling and multi-session serving. We introduce TickTock-Bench, benchmark and replay harness for decoding in chunk-interleaved full-duplex models, which enables comparison of decoding methods under the same chunk deadlines. 2. Related Work Full-duplex speech language models. They listen and speak at the same time. Moshi (Defossez et al., 2024) modeled the users speech and its own as parallel streams. Chunk-interleaved models arranged input and output in one causal sequence: Zhang et al. (2024b) split the dialogue into time slices, OmniFlatten (Zhang et al., 2025) flattened the streams into single sequence, and MiniCPM-o 4.5 (Cui et al., 2026) and the interaction model of Thinking Machines Lab (2026) processed streaming dialogue in fixed-duration chunks. Gander (Orantqing et al., 2026) and Realtime-Venus (Ant Group, 2026) added tool calls and external delegation to the stream, and LWS (Zhang et al., 2026) added written channel that can be decoded in the same chunk as speech. Speculative decoding. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) drafted several tokens cheaply and verified them in one forward pass of the target model, which preserves its output distribution. Drafts came from smaller model, from heads trained on the targets hidden states as in Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) and EAGLE (Li et al., 2024), or from subset of the target models own layers, as in Draft & Verify (Zhang et al., 2024a) and Kangaroo (Liu et al., 2024). Training-free methods drafted without extra parameters: prompt lookup decoding (PLD) (Saxena, 2023) matched n-grams in the context, Token Recycling (Luo et al., 2025) reused candidate tokens from earlier decoding steps, and lookahead decoding (Fu et al., 2024) collected n-grams from Jacobi iterations in pool. Spec-Bench (Xia et al., 2024) compared these methods under unified protocol for text generation. In spoken dialogue, speculative generation was used to start responses earlier: RelayS2S (Mai & Liang, 2026) let fast duplex model draft the opening of response that cascaded pipeline can continue, and SpecS2 Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models Figure 2. Overview of Speculative Listening. Observation 1 motivates drafting under silence and verifying the draft in the audio prefill pass. Observation 2 motivates runner-up branch at the first token and hypothesis pool for later forward passes to continue from. peak (Jiang et al., 2026) started speech synthesis from draft tokens while the target model verified them. These methods draft once the input is available; Speculative Listening is training-free self-speculative method that drafts the output of chunk before its audio arrives. Computing ahead of the input. Human speakers plan their response while still listening, which keeps the gap between turns near 200 ms (Levinson & Torreira, 2015). Speech systems have used the listening time in several ways. Chronological Thinking (Wu et al., 2026) trained fullduplex model to emit reasoning tokens while listening. PredGen (Li & Grover, 2025) pre-generated candidate responses from partial user input in cascaded pipeline. Saguaro (Kumar et al., 2026) prepared speculations for likely verification outcomes while the current verification was still running. These methods compute ahead of their input with extra training, cascaded pipeline, or separate draft model; Speculative Listening drafts the next chunk with the unchanged model and verifies it against the real audio. 3. Method In this section, we formalize decoding in chunkinterleaved model, report two observations on chunk outputs, and present Speculative Listening. 3.1. Preliminary: Chunk-Interleaved Decoding chunk-interleaved model divides conversation into time chunks = 1, 2, . . . of fixed duration. Let at denote the input tokens of chunk t, namely the encoded audio of the chunk together with any concurrent text input, and let yt denote its output tokens. The model processes all chunks as one causal sequence, and the context of chunk is x<t = (a1, y1, . . . , at1, yt1). Within chunk, we drop the chunk index and write yt = (y1, . . . , yyt) with yi V. In most models, the first token y1 decides whether the model keeps listening or starts an output, through an explicit listen/speak token in some models (Cui et al., 2026; Orantqing et al., 2026) and an end-of-chunk token in others; the remaining tokens carry the content, such as text for speech decoder or structured tool call. Under greedy decoding, model with parameters θ generates yi = arg max yV pθ (y x<t, at, y<i) . (1) forward pass of the model processes block of input tokens and yields the distribution of the next token at each position. Autoregressive decoding prefills at and then decodes the output token by token. Each forward pass takes the token decoded by the previous one as input, and the forward passes run one after another. Their number after at arrives grows linearly with yt. forward pass over few tokens takes about as long as forward pass over one token (Shazeer, 2019; Kim et al., 2023). We call the time from the arrival of at to the end of the chunks computation its post-audio latency. chunk whose post-audio latency exceeds the chunk duration misses its deadline and delays the following chunks. Chunk profile. We profiled autoregressive decoding by chunk type on the four models of Section 5.1 (Figure 3a). Listen chunks process the audio and output only control tokens, and compute waits for the next audio during 7089% of the chunk duration. We call this time the idle window. Speak and tool-call chunks sit at the other end. tool call takes tens of serial forward passes and completes 1.82.6 after its audio arrives, and every evaluated tool call missed the deadline. Observations Using the idle window requires decoding chunk before at arrives, that is, under an assumed input. We take silence as the simplest assumption: the silence hypothesis replaces at with asil, the input tokens of chunk of silence with no text input. To measure how often it yields the real output, we ran an oracle probe without time limit. It decodes every chunk twice, once with at and once with asil, and checks whether the two outputs are identical (Figure 3b,c). Observation 1: the next audio chunk usually does not change the output. Pooled over the four models, the two outputs match in 95.3% of chunks. The match rate is lowest on Realtime-Venus while the user is speaking, when incoming speech updates the context (Figure 3b and Section B.2). Observation 2: changes concentrate at the first token. Pooled over the four models, 87.7% of mismatched chunks diverge at the first output token, which in most models is the decision to keep listening or to start an output (Figure 3c). 3.3. Speculative Listening Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) drafts the next few tokens and feeds the whole draft to the target model as input in one forward pass. In this forward pass, the distribution for the i-th token depends only on the first 1 draft tokens. When these tokens are correct, it equals the distribution of autoregressive decoding at step i. Verification accepts the draft tokens up to the first mismatch and replaces the mismatched token with the choice of the target model. single forward pass can then commit several tokens, and it takes about as long as decoding one token (Section 3.1). Speculative Listening uses the target model itself as the draft model and drafts chunk under the silence hypothesis during the idle window, before at arrives. It verifies the draft in the forward pass prefilling at (Figure 2). The forward passes of drafting run before the audio arrives. When the draft matches the whole output, the number of post-audio forward passes no longer grows with yt. Drafting under the silence hypothesis. Following greedy verification (Xia et al., 2024), the number of accepted tokens is = min ({ 1 1 γ, yi = arg max pi } {γ}) . Every forward pass commits at least one token, and the number of post-audio forward passes never exceeds the number under autoregressive decoding. TickTock-Bench In this section, we introduce TickTock-Bench, benchmark for evaluating decoding methods on chunk-interleaved fullduplex models. In these models, the chunk duration acts as hard deadline: chunk that takes longer to decode delays the following chunks, and the conversation lags behind real time. The model then processes the users speech late, and its responses become stale in the ongoing interaction. The value of decoding method for these models lies in how it changes this behaviour: how long response or tool call waits after the users audio, how often chunks miss their deadlines, and how far the conversation falls behind. Measuring these effects requires checking each chunk against its deadline, by chunk type, in the models own runtime. Chunk-interleaved models are also growing in number, each with its own runtime, and shared benchmark lets decoding methods be compared across them. Following Spec-Bench (Xia et al., 2024), which compared speculative decoding methods on text generation under unified protocol, TickTock-Bench evaluates all methods on the same sessions and hardware under this chunk-level measurement. We release it for evaluating future decoding methods on these models in the same way. TickTock-Bench covers three task categories  (Table 1)  : speech reasoning with Web Questions (Berant et al., 2013), Llama Questions (Nachmani et al., 2024), and TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) from OpenAudioBench (Li et al., 2025), AlpacaEval from VoiceBench (Chen et al., 2024), and Big Bench Audio (BBA) (Artificial Analysis, 2024; Srivastava et al., 2022; Suzgun et al., 2023); conversational dynamics with Full-Duplex-Bench (FDB) v1 (Lin et al., 2025) and v1.5 (Lin et al., 2026b); and agentic tool use with FDB v3 (Lin et al., 2026a). Speech reasoning tests spoken question answering, conversational dynamics tests listening and responding around pauses, turn ends, and overlapping speech, and agentic tool use tests tool calls. The replay harness feeds each session to the model chunk by chunk through its own runtime, one session at time on one NVIDIA A100 GPU, and labels each chunk by its output as listen, speak, or tool-call chunk. We use the speedup over autoregressive decoding in mean post-audio latency per chunk type as the primary metric, measured in wall-clock time without speech synthesis. Computation that method performs before the audio arrives runs in the idle window, and any part beyond the idle window is added to the post-audio latency. To measure how far decoding falls behind real time, we also report the deadline miss rate and the maximum lag behind the audio per session, together with #MAT (Xia et al., 2024). Details are provided in Section A. 5. Experiments 5.1. Experimental Setup Evaluation. On FDB v3, we reported tool-call chunks for Streaming SLM and Gander, and speak chunks for RealtimeVenus and LWS. Realtime-Venus issued no tool calls on these sessions under greedy decoding, and LWS has no toolcall channel. The ablation and the analysis use FDB v3 and Llama Questions. All evaluated methods are lossless: in exact arithmetic, their outputs are identical to those of autoregressive decoding (Section 5.4). Models. In all four models, the backbone (Thinker) decodes text tokens, and separate speech decoder (Talker) synthesizes the audio from these tokens or their hidden states. We measured the Thinker only, since it is the only component in which the methods differ. Baselines. We compared Speculative Listening with autoregressive decoding (AR) and three training-free, modelfree speculative decoding methods that run after the audio arrives. Prompt Lookup Decoding (PLD) (Saxena, 2023) drafts tokens by matching n-grams in the context. Token Recycling (Luo et al., 2025) drafts from candidate tokens recycled from earlier decoding steps, and lookahead decoding (Fu et al., 2024) drafts from n-grams collected by Jacobi iterations; we evaluated both in chain verification mode to match the models runtimes. Implementation. All models ran in bfloat16 with greedy decoding and batch size 1, under the protocol of Section 4. 5.2. Main Results Speedup across models and tasks. By drafting in the idle window and verifying in the audio forward pass, Speculative Listening decodes most of chunks output before its audio arrives. Deadline misses. We further examined whether Speculative Listening keeps the models in real time. deadline miss delays the following chunks, and the delay accumulates over consecutive chunks. To quantify this effect, we measured the maximum lag behind the audio per session (Section A). As shown in Table 3, under AR the maximum lag reaches 2.6 on Streaming SLM and 4.0 on LWS, and 35% of the sessions of Streaming SLM lag behind the audio by more than 1 s. With Speculative Listening, the lag stays at zero on Streaming SLM and Realtime-Venus and averages 42 ms on Gander and 55 ms on LWS, and at most 1% of the sessions lag behind the audio by more than 1 s. These results show that Speculative Listening reduces the maximum lag behind real time by 94.4% on average. 5.3. Ablation Study To examine the contribution of each component, we added silence-hypothesis drafting, the hypothesis pool, and the runner-up branch to AR one at time on Streaming SLM and Gander, using FDB v3 for tool-call chunks and Llama Questions for speak chunks. Effects of silence-hypothesis drafting. We first added silence-hypothesis drafting alone. As shown in Table 4, it speeds up speak chunks by 2.62.9 and tool-call chunks by 1.21.4. These results show that drafting within one idle window covers short outputs. tool call of several dozen tokens exceeds the idle window, and its draft stops before the call is complete. Effects of the hypothesis pool. We then added the hypothesis pool. As shown in Table 4, it raises the tool-call speedup from 1.42 to 22.04 on Streaming SLM and from 1.21 to 2.04 on Gander. These results show that drafts from earlier chunks cover most of tool call: user request spans several chunks, and the drafts made in earlier chunks already contain most of the eventual call. Effects of the runner-up branch. Finally, we added the runner-up branch. As shown in Table 4, it raises the toolcall speedup from 2.04 to 3.45 on Gander and from 22.04 to 23.41 on Streaming SLM. These results show that the branch helps where the silence draft departs at the first token (Observation 2): it provides draft starting from the alternative first token. On Streaming SLM, the pool already leaves little for the branch to remove. 7 Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models Figure 5. Case study of user-perceived latency. SL: Speculative Listening. (a) Response onset. Under AR, speech starts after the last token of the chunk is decoded. With Speculative Listening, the draft made under silence is verified when the audio arrives, and speech starts earlier. (b) Tool call. Under AR, long tool call runs past the deadline and delays the next chunk. With Speculative Listening, the call drafted in earlier chunks is verified from the hypothesis pool and is ready within the chunk. 5.4. In-Depth Analysis Analysis on user-perceived latency. To examine whether the speedup shortens the delays that users hear, we measured two latencies (Figure 5 and Section C). The response onset latency is the time from the arrival of the audio of the first speak chunk of response to the end of its Thinker output. The tool-call latency is the time from the arrival of the audio of tool-call chunk to the end of the call. As shown in Table 5, Speculative Listening reduces the response onset latency by 73% on average across the four models and the tool-call latency by 7296%. These results show that the post-audio speedup shortens the delays before response and before tool call. Human speakers start response about 200 ms after the other speaker ends (Levinson & Torreira, 2015). Under AR, decoding alone adds 4171089 ms before response starts. With Speculative Listening, it adds 74241 ms, close to this gap, and tool calls become ready within the chunk duration on average. Analysis on output length and sampling. To examine whether the speedup holds beyond the main setting, we varied the output length and the sampling temperature {0.3, 0.7, 1.0} (Figure 4a,b). With Speculative Listening, chunk needs 1.01.4 post-audio forward passes for outputs of 2 to 128 tokens. AR grows from 2.0 passes for one token to 73.6 passes for 65128 tokens, the three baselines follow the same trend, and silence-hypothesis drafting alone reaches 52.9 passes. Speculative Listening speeds up speak and tool-call chunks by 2.1 and 13.3 at = 0.3 and by 1.4 and 5.4 at = 1.0. Sampled tokens depart from the greedy draft more often as the temperature rises and shorten the accepted prefix. These results show that Speculative Listening needs few post-audio passes at every output length and remains effective under sampling. Analysis on response quality. To examine whether Speculative Listening preserves the outputs of AR, we compared the two. Under float32, Speculative Listening reproduces AR token for token on nearly all sessions. Under bfloat16, used in the main tables, rounding can change outputs, and 8 the AlpacaEval judge scores of AR and Speculative Listening differ by less than 0.1 point on all four models (Table 6 in Section B.1). These results show that Speculative Listening preserves the response quality of AR. 6. Conclusion and Future Work In this work, we studied decoding latency in chunkinterleaved full-duplex speech language models. We identified an asymmetric workload across chunks: listen chunks leave compute idle while awaiting audio, and speak and toolcall chunks require serial generation growing with output length. Comparing outputs under real audio and the silence hypothesis, we found two properties: the next audio chunk usually does not change the output, and changes concentrate at the first token. Building on these properties, we proposed Speculative Listening, training-free and lossless framework. It drafts each chunk in the idle window and verifies the draft in the audio forward pass. On TickTock-Bench, it reduces the maximum lag behind real time by 94.4% and the decoding delay before response starts by 73% on average. Future work includes drafting under input hypotheses beyond digital silence, such as streaming acoustic features.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: This work has three limitations. First, Speculative Listening targets low-concurrency, latency-sensitive deployment. It computes during the idle window, and the idle window shrinks as more sessions share GPU or are batched. In our multi-session experiment, concurrent sessions share one GPU, and the speedup decreases as the number of sessions grows (Section B.4). Second, we compared the Thinker only, since the Talkers of the four models synthesize speech in different ways and would confound the comparison. Third, our formulation targets chunk-interleaved architectures with an idle window between chunks; parallel-stream architectures such as Moshi (Defossez et al., 2024), which decode at every 80 ms audio frame, require different formulation. Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models

B.4. Multi-Session Serving To examine Speculative Listening under GPU contention, we ran {1, 2, 4} concurrent sessions on one A100 GPU and measured wall-clock latency. As shown in Figure 4c, at = 1 Speculative Listening speeds up speak chunks by 2.9 and tool-call chunks by 22.7. At = 4, it speeds up speak chunks by 2.0 and tool-call chunks by 10.5, and it reduces the 12 Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models deadline miss rate of tool-call chunks from 100% to 2.9%. These results show that Speculative Listening remains effective under GPU contention, and its gain on long tool calls decreases as grows. Concurrent sessions slow down drafting, which leaves less time to draft long tool calls. C. Case Study To illustrate how Speculative Listening shortens the delays that users perceive (Wang et al., 2026b; Ao et al., 2026), we walk through two example sessions in Figure 6. The latencies in the figure are typical values measured on TickTock-Bench  (Table 5)  . Figure 6. Case study on two illustrative sessions. SL: Speculative Listening. Span labels give typical measured latencies  (Table 5)  , and green spans mark the time saved by Speculative Listening. Check marks denote drafted tokens accepted by verification. (a) Response onset. The first speak chunk is drafted under silence in chunk 2 and verified when its audio arrives. (b) Tool call. R: tool result. Drafts made while the user speaks contain the tool call and enter the hypothesis pool. Under AR, the call misses the deadline, and the dashed arrow links the audio of chunk 5 to the time AR starts processing it. Response onset. As shown in Figure 6a, the user asks question in chunks 1 and 2, and the model starts its answer in chunk 3. Under AR, the model decodes the first speak chunk after its audio arrives, and the output is ready after 0.9 s. With Speculative Listening, the model drafts chunk 3 under silence during the idle window of chunk 2, and the audio forward pass of chunk 3 verifies the draft. The output is ready after 0.2 s. In chunks 4 to 6, both methods finish each speak chunk within the chunk duration, and each chunk starts when its audio arrives. The answer then streams at the same pace under both methods and starts 0.7 earlier with Speculative Listening. Tool call. As shown in Figure 6b, the user requests flight over chunks 1 to 3. During each idle window, Speculative Listening drafts the next chunk under silence. From chunk 2 on, these drafts contain the tool call with the details heard so far, and the hypothesis pool keeps them. While the user is still speaking, verification rejects them at the first token. In chunk 4, the audio forward pass verifies the drafted call, and the call is ready after 0.1 s. Under AR, the model decodes the call token by token for 2.6 and misses the deadline by 1.6 s. Chunk 5 then starts 1.6 after its audio arrives. In this example, the tool returns its result 0.5 after the call is dispatched, and the result enters the first chunk that starts after it returns (Wang et al., 2026a; Shen et al., 2026). It enters chunk 5 with Speculative Listening and chunk 7 under AR. The answer to the user then starts 2.2 earlier with Speculative Listening.
